title: Λέων ⟨ἐγκλεισθεὶς⟩ καὶ γεωργός
titleEn: The Lion Shut In and the Farmer
part: The Lion Shut In and the Farmer (Chambry 197)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 197. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A lion went into a farmer's steading.
sentences.n: ἔπαυλις is the walled farmyard with its byres and folds — one gate, and everything of value inside it. The angle brackets in Chambry's title, ⟨ἐγκλεισθείς⟩, mark his own supplement; it distinguishes this fable from the next, which carries the same title otherwise.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ συλλαβεῖν βουλόμενος τὴν αὔλειαν θύραν ἔκλεισε.
sentences.tr: Ho de syllabein boulomenos tēn auleian thyran ekleise.
sentences.l: And he, wishing to catch him, shut the courtyard door.
sentences.n: ἡ αὔλειος θύρα is the outer door of the yard, the one that shuts the whole place. συλλαβεῖν is 'to seize, take'; the farmer means to have the lion, and shutting the gate is the whole of his plan.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς ἐξελθεῖν μὴ δυνάμενος πρῶτον μὲν τὰ ποίμνια διέφθειρεν, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς βόας ἐτράπη.
sentences.tr: Kai hos exelthein mē dynamenos prōton men ta poimnia diephtheiren, epeita de kai epi tous boas etrapē.
sentences.l: And he, not being able to get out, first destroyed the flocks, and then turned upon the oxen as well.
sentences.n: καὶ ὅς, 'and he', is the old demonstrative use of the relative pronoun, kept alive in narrative for a change of subject. μέν … δέ carries the escalation: sheep first, then the oxen, which are the farm's capital.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ γεωργὸς φοβηθεὶς περὶ αὐτοῦ τὴν θύραν ἀνέῳξεν.
sentences.tr: Kai ho geōrgos phobētheis peri autou tēn thyran aneōixen.
sentences.l: And the farmer, having taken fright for himself, opened the door.
sentences.n: περὶ αὐτοῦ is printed without the rough breathing that would mark it as reflexive (αὑτοῦ); the sense is nevertheless the farmer's own skin — with the flocks gone and the oxen going, he is what is left.

sentences.t: Ἀπαλλαγέντος δὲ τοῦ λέοντος, ἡ γυνὴ θεασαμένη αὐτὸν στένοντα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλὰ σύ γε δίκαια πέπονθας· τί γὰρ τοῦτον συγκλεῖσαι ἐβούλου ὃν καὶ μακρόθεν σε ἔδει φεύγειν ; »
sentences.tr: Apallagentos de tou leontos, hē gynē theasamenē auton stenonta eipen· « Alla sy ge dikaia peponthas· ti gar touton synkleisai eboulou hon kai makrothen se edei pheugein ; »
sentences.l: And the lion having got away, the farmer's wife, seeing him groaning, said: « But you at any rate have suffered justly; for why did you want to shut this one in, from whom you ought to have fled even at a distance? »
sentences.i: When the lion had made off, the farmer's wife saw him groaning and said: « You have suffered no more than you deserved. Why did you want to shut in a beast you should have run from while he was still far away? »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute opens the sentence, the fable's usual way of clearing one scene before the next. δίκαια πέπονθας, 'you have suffered just things', is the standing Greek way of saying that a man has got what was coming to him. ἔδει, imperfect, states an obligation that was not met: 'you ought to have fled', and did not.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ τοὺς ἰσχυροτέρους διερεθίζοντες εἰκότως τὰς ἐξ αὐτῶν πλημμελείας ὑπομένουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi tous ischyroterous dierethizontes eikotōs tas ex autōn plēmmeleias hypomenousin.
sentences.l: Thus those who provoke the stronger, as is only to be expected, put up with the outrages that come from them.
sentences.i: Thus it is only to be expected that those who go out of their way to provoke the stronger should have to bear the injuries that come to them from that quarter.
sentences.n: διερεθίζω has the intensive διά: not merely to irritate, but to work a thing up thoroughly. πλημμέλεια is borrowed from music — the false note, the thing played out of tune — and stands here for the whole disorder a wronged power lets loose.
